name: Modulation
seoDesc: Modulation: work out carrier signal amplitude (Ac) from the message signal amplitude and the amplitude modulation index. A free physics calculator with…
summary: Give the Modulation calculator the message signal amplitude, the amplitude modulation index, the max frequency deviation and the frequency modulation index and it returns carrier signal amplitude (Ac). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Modulation calculator work?
sections.html:
The Modulation calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports carrier signal amplitude (Ac) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the message signal amplitude (Aₘ), the amplitude modulation index (μₐ), the max frequency deviation (Δf) and the frequency modulation index (μf).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as amplitude and frequency. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hertz. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Modulation calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Carrier signal amplitude (Ac)=message signal amplitude (Aₘ) ÷ amplitude modulation index (μₐ)
Message signal frequency (fₘ)=max frequency deviation (Δf) ÷ frequency modulation index (μf)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Calculate modulation index of set to amplitude, Message signal amplitude (Aₘ) = 10 V and Amplitude modulation index (μₐ) = 10. The calculator returns Carrier signal amplitude (Ac) = 1 V.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Carrier signal amplitude (Ac) = 1 V should be roughly the size you expected from Calculate modulation index of set to amplitude and Message signal amplitude (Aₘ) = 10 V.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in hertz, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Frequency, opening in hertz

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Modulation calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the message signal amplitude, the amplitude modulation index and the max frequency deviation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Modulation calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns carrier signal amplitude (Ac), derived from the message signal amplitude, the amplitude modulation index and the max frequency deviation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Modulation calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the message signal amplitude, the amplitude modulation index, the max frequency deviation and the frequency modulation index, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter message signal amplitude (Aₘ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Message signal amplitude (Aₘ) opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Carrier signal amplitude (Ac) = 1 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Modulation calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
